title: heterogeneous-priority-queues-and-soft-quotas-for-rerank-latency
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: The reranking endpoint is experiencing tail latency spikes during mixed workloads: long-candidate requests (many tokens) block short low-latency scoring requests. Existing single-queue admission and naive batching cause head-of-line blocking, increased latency P95/P99, and inconsistent quality when soft timeouts trigger early exits. Goal: reduce tail latency for latency-sensitive rerank requests while preserving throughput and score quality for bulk/long requests.

Proposal summary: Introduce heterogeneous priority queues (HPQ) with soft quotas and deadline-aware admission. HPQ partitions incoming rerank requests into three lanes by estimated token budget and SLO: fast (<=8 tokens, latency-first), balanced (9-64 tokens), and heavy (>64 tokens). Each lane has its own micro-batching pool and a configurable soft quota that controls concurrent in-flight token budgets. If fast lane soft quota is saturated, a bounded short-term overflow policy allows limited borrowing from balanced lane with preemptible microbatches. Implement deadline-aware timeouts and escalation: each request carries an attached deadline derived from route SLO; timeouts cascade from soft timeouts (graceful re-score / partial results) to hard timeouts (abort). Add speculative short-circuiting for fast lane: run a lightweight early-filter model (cheap embedding or linear scorer) to prefilter obvious negatives so heavy ops don't enter critical path.

Design decisions and trade-offs: 1) Number of lanes: three lanes chosen to balance implementation complexity and coverage of common token distributions observed in production. More lanes increase scheduling overhead. 2) Soft quotas vs hard caps: soft quotas improve utilization by allowing temporary borrowing but introduce complexity in fairness; use probabilistic admission to avoid starvation. 3) KV cache hints: accept an optional kv_hint field to surface whether a request is cacheable or cold; cached requests go to a dedicated fast path micro-pool to reduce memory churn. 4) Speculative prefilter accuracy vs cost: small model must be tuned to avoid hurting final ranking quality; initial rollout will use conservative thresholds and monitor precision/recall on held-out evals.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Stage A: Scheduler + lanes (server-side routing only)
  - Add HPQ scheduler service that tags requests into lanes using token_estimate and route config.
  - Implement per-lane microbatch pools and executor threads.
  - Telemetry hooks: per-lane enqueue latency, microbatch size distribution, soft quota utilization.
- Stage B: Soft quotas and overflow borrowing
  - Implement soft quota accounting by token budget and active microbatches.
  - Borrowing policy: allow N% of balanced tokens to be temporarily used for fast lane if backlog exceeds threshold and predicted latency breach probability > X.
- Stage C: Deadline escalation and partial scoring
  - Wire request deadlines; implement graceful partial scoring (e.g., run first k candidates and return partial ranked list with confidence tags).
  - Add metrics to track partial vs full returns and user-visible quality delta.
- Stage D: Speculative prefilter and KV hints
  - Integrate a small prefilter model and KV hint pipeline.
  - Add canary tests to verify ranking parity.
- Stage E: Rollout & tuning
  - Canary 1: 2% of traffic (non-paid customers), monitor latency P50/P95/P99, accuracy delta on evaluation prompts, and token throughput.
  - Canary 2: 20% of traffic with alerting thresholds tightened.
  - Full rollout after 2 weeks of stable metrics and sign-off.

Testing and success metrics:
- Latency: reduce rerank P99 by >=35% on mixed workload; P95 reduction >=20% for fast lane routes.
- Quality: measured change in rerank NDCG@10 <= 0.5% absolute degradation on production eval set for any route.
- Throughput: overall token throughput should not drop by more than 7% at steady state.
- Observability: per-lane dashboards for queue depth, soft quota utilization, borrow events, and partial-return ratio.

Backward compatibility and fallbacks:
- If HPQ shows regression, route can be disabled per-customer/route flag.
- On failures in the scheduler, default to single-queue legacy path.
- Maintain telemetry parity with current endpoints for postmortem comparison.

Rollout checklist and runbook pointers:
- Feature flag gates per region and per-customer.
- Dashboards: rerank/hpq/* (queue depth, latency by lane, borrow rate, partial returns).
- SLO alerts: lane-specific P95/P99 thresholds.
- Runbook: link to incident playbook (confluence) and steps to revert service flag.

Open questions and risks:
- Estimating token budget from request metadata is noisy; misclassification could push short requests to heavy lane. Mitigation: conservative thresholds + dynamic calibration using online histograms.
- Speculative prefilter false negatives may lower final quality; will gate by conservative thresholds and A/B evals.
- Soft borrowing parameters need careful tuning to prevent oscillation; will use PID-like smoothing.

References & artifacts:
- Design doc draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/rerank-hpq-design (internal)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rerank/pull/812 (backend scheduler)
- Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rerank-hpq (canary panels)
